crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Harmonising Privacy Frameworks
children.blurb: Harmonising privacy frameworks is the work of aligning two or more data protection regimes so that a single set of practices can satisfy all of them at once.

children.name: Incident Response and Breach Notification
children.blurb: Incident response and breach notification covers the process an organisation follows when personal data or a system is compromised, from detection through containment, assessment, notification and post-incident review.

children.name: Cross-Border Data Transfers
children.blurb: Cross-border data transfers covers the movement of personal and often sensitive data from one jurisdiction to another, whether by a company sending records to a foreign subsidiary, a cloud provider storing data in a data centre abroad, or a model developer pulling training data across regions.

children.name: AI Supply Chain Liability
children.blurb: AI supply chain liability concerns who bears responsibility when an AI system causes harm and the components behind it came from several different vendors.

children.name: Biometric and Surveillance Law
children.blurb: Biometric and surveillance law covers the rules that govern collecting, storing, and using data tied to a person's body or behaviour, including fingerprints, face geometry, iris patterns, voiceprints, gait, and licence plate reads.

sections.body: This section covers the legal work that sits between artificial intelligence systems and the rules governing personal data. In practice, privacy teams now spend their time mapping where training data came from, writing data protection impact assessments for models that touch personal information, and negotiating contracts with vendors whose models were built on data the buyer never saw. Breach response has changed too, because an incident involving a model or an inference endpoint raises questions about what was actually exposed and who has to be told. Biometric systems, from facial recognition to voice analysis, sit at the sharp end of this work because they process data that cannot be reissued the way a password can. The section treats these as operational problems, not abstract principles.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are settled. Notification clocks, processor contracts and the basic mechanics of a subject access request are well understood, and most organisations have run them many times. What is not settled is how privacy law applies to models themselves, whether a trained model counts as personal data, what deletion means when data has been absorbed into weights, and how liability is shared across a supply chain of foundation model providers, fine tuners and deployers. Regulators have issued guidance but few binding decisions, and courts are still working through the early cases. The honest limit is that compliance here is often a judgement call made without clear precedent, and the volume of new state legislation means the ground keeps moving. This site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which gives a sense of how much is still being argued rather than decided.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Harmonising Privacy Frameworks to understand how differing national and regional regimes are being reconciled, or not, and what that means for a single compliance programme. Incident Response and Breach Notification takes that baseline and applies it to the moment something goes wrong, covering who must be told, when, and what evidence has to be preserved. Cross-Border Data Transfers deals with moving data between jurisdictions, including the adequacy and contractual mechanisms that make transfers lawful. AI Supply Chain Liability follows the chain outward to vendors and model providers, asking who answers when a component fails or a model misbehaves. Biometric and Surveillance Law closes the set by focusing on the category of data that attracts the strictest rules and the most litigation. Together they move from framework to incident to transfer to supply chain to the most sensitive data type, which is roughly the order a compliance team encounters them.
